newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Dow plunge, weak currencies roil Asia stocks.
newsitem.headline: Dow plunge, weak currencies roil Asia stocks.

text.p: Wall Street's staggering drop and continued attacks on local currencies sent tremors through already jittery Asian markets on Monday, taking stocks sharply lower across the region.
Tokyo stocks lost over two percent, while those in Indonesia were down more than eight percent.
"It's the old adage, when Wall Street coughs everybody else catches a cold," said Tim Koller at Merrill Lynch in Wellington, NZ.

On Friday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 247.37 points, or 3.11 percent, to close at 7,694.66. It was the second largest point loss in the market's history, and brought the loss for the week to more than 330 points.
The Dow is now 6.8 percent below its all-time closing high of 8,259.31 set on August 6.
"Because the U.S. is such a big part of the world economy, everyone will be waiting to see whether they have a rally or not," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Sydney institutional head Marlon Freeman.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225-share index fell 391.74 points, or 2.03 percent, at midday to 18,934.29 before recovering slightly. It was off 351.63 points, or 1.82 percent at 0345 GMT.
Most of the selloff in Tokyo was in the electronics sector, which had rallied recently.
Keiko Kondo, a strategist at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc said: "The Japanese market is currently vulnerable to negative news because of the shaky recovery in the domestic economy."

Indonesian stocks posted the largest percentage loss in the region, with the composite index dropping 51.19 points, or 8.29 percent, to 566.52 amid widespread unease over the weakness in the rupiah and an increase in margin calls.
Philippine stocks also fell sharply. The composite index down 100.83 points, or 4.12 percent to 2,348.10 points.
The Dow's drop triggered an early selloff which brought the market below the 2,400 support level, but subsequent losses came as the bearish mood dragged the peso to a record low of 30 to the dollar.

"The market is so bearish that any bad news such as the Dow's fall is magnified. Add to that the continued turmoil in the currency...," said Noel Reyes, vice- president at Anscor-Hagedorn Securities in Manila.

In Malaysia, where last week the ringgit fell to its lowest level since it was officially floated in 1973, the Dow's fall triggered selling in stocks. The market had lost 3.11 percent in early trading, before recovering slightly to be down 18.13 points, or 2.00 percent, at 891.99.
Thai stocks lost 7.52 points, or 1.21 percent, in early trade to stand at 615.73, while Singapore's Straits Times Index was down 44.67 points, or 2.29 percent, at 1,909.13.
South Korean stocks fell victim to financial troubles at another large corporation, textile marker Han Joo, with stocks falling 1.06 points to 747.35.
Australian stocks were off the day's lows. "We're recovering quite well, but we're not going to rally this afternoon," said one senior trader in Sydney.
The All Ordinaries Index was down 57.8 points, or 2.17 percent at 2,608.4, while New Zealand shares were down 24.81 points, or 0.99 percent, at 2,470.82.
